identity.real_world_identity_notes: Reiza's fictional entry-level open-wheel car, described as a category intended for new racing drivers with a car that appears to be based on the Formula Ford.

wheel_rim.notes: Observed from the cockpit during the guided drive.

notes: Simulator behaviour was directly observed in a guided drive in AMS2 1.6.9.91 with automatic clutch and shifting disabled: automatic cut on upshifts and no automatic blip on downshifts. The downshift was accepted with no pedal input, so no blip is needed to engage the gear, and a clutch is still needed to pull away.

The gearbox is widely reported as an H-pattern, including in community summaries, and it is not. A Reiza internal tester explains that an H-shifter can be bound to a sequential gearbox in game as an accommodation for players without sequential hardware, and that the selection menu does not state transmissions, which is what the mistake comes from. The drive read the gearbox rather than the menu.

This class reports a single aero configuration. The selection screen offers no high or low downforce package, and only the plain identity has ever been observed, so there is no further identity to carry.
The car does not blip its own downshifts. An earlier drive recorded that it did, from a measurement that could read the driver's throttle as the car's blip.
Observed live in AMS2 1.6.9.91 via guided verification observation ams2.formula-trainer-advanced.20260815t193525122z-0e83d30a by Jason Kinslow.

The automatic blip was re-measured on 2026-08-18 in AMS2 1.6.9.91, observation ams2.formula-trainer-advanced.20260818t035006434z-59e6a110. The car does not blip: the first reading was the old measurement seeing throttle carried in before the lift. The downshift was still accepted with no pedal input, so no blip is needed to engage the gear.

confidence.basis: Simulator behaviour was live-tested in AMS2 1.6.9.91 with automatic clutch and shifting disabled, and the real-world transmission is supported by registered sources.

claims.basis: The identity is Reiza's own model name, observed exactly in live telemetry; no real-world chassis identity is assigned.

The live drive selected four gears through a sequential stick with an automatic cut and no automatic blip. A Reiza forum thread resolves the recurring question about this car: a member who tested it states it is definitely sequential, for both the Trainer and the Trainer Advanced.
Directly observed during the guided drive: move-off, shift clutch use, automatic cut and blip, and the cockpit rim.

driver_summary: Sequential stick, one gear at a time. The car cuts the upshift, and nothing blips the downshift, though the gear will engage unmatched. Blip anyway: it is the difference between the car settling into the corner and the driven wheels locking as you turn in.
